transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Nina Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Asha Rao (CTO, Veridian), Marc Nguyen (ML Lead), Leah Ortiz (DevOps), Tom Reed (Product)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. I'm Samir from Redwood, with Nina and Jordan from our solutions team. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Asha: Doing well, thanks. Busy end of quarter but excited to talk through migration options.
[00:12] Samir: Great. Quick agenda — understand your current stack and pain points with OpenAI, talk about Dedicated and Private options, compatibility questions especially around vLLM/TGI and eval parity, and agree next steps. Sound good?
[00:20] Marc: Yep that's perfect.
[00:23] Samir: Cool, can you give a quick rundown of your current setup and why you're exploring a move?
[00:30] Marc: Sure. We run a mix of real-time chat completions and batch embedding jobs. Right now everything's on OpenAI's API. We're hitting a few issues: spikes in latency during peak traffic, and cost unpredictability as usage scales. Also we need more control for compliance — some customers require data residency and auditability.
[00:44] Asha: To add, we also run local experiments with vLLM/TGI on prem when we need custom kernels or quantized runs. But those are experimental and not stable for production. We're looking at Redwood because we want the predictability of reserved capacity but don't want to rebuild all our infra.
[01:00] Nina: Thanks, that's helpful. A couple clarifying q's — what's your target latency for interactive chat and what's your throughput pattern?
[01:06] Marc: Target is sub-200ms 95p for short-turn prompts (<100 tokens). Peak throughput 600 req/s with bursts to 1.2k for short windows. Embeddings are bulk nightly jobs but cost matters.
[01:18] Jordan: Good notes. On compatibility — you mentioned vLLM/TGI experiments. Is your inference code directly calling those runtimes, or do you wrap them behind an adapter layer?
[01:26] Marc: We have a small adapter so we can swap runtimes, but tokenization differences and a few micro-differences in sampling make parity testing annoying.
[01:34] Samir: That's common. For Dedicated, our runtime exposes a REST/SDK interface similar to hosted, and you can bring models in a few ways — we support open model weights and provide a conversion guide. For vLLM/TGI, Redwood can run models compiled to our optimized kernels; we also provide a vLLM compatibility matrix.
[01:49] Marc: Can you run TGI artifacts as-is or do we need to repackage?
[01:53] Nina: Short answer: often repackage. Some TGI runtimes are pretty close, but we recommend a quick conversion step plus a tiny shim in a few cases. We'll share the conversion script. There can be tokenization mismatches if you switch tokenizers — that causes eval drift.
[02:08] Marc: Eval drift is our biggest fear. Our product relies on model outputs being very consistent — subtle changes break downstream heuristics. How do you help with eval parity vs OpenAI?
[02:18] Jordan: We do a few things: first, we run side-by-side evals using your prompt suite — we can provision dedicated capacity to reproduce your peak profile and run both OpenAI and Redwood models. Second, we support model variants and rollbacks to quickly revert if something regresses. Third, we provide tools to pin sampling and temperature compatibility.
[02:36] Asha: That benchmarking offer sounds useful. What's the SLA/perf difference between Hosted and Dedicated — particularly for latency and tail latency?
[02:44] Samir: Hosted provides fast onboarding but is multi-tenant and subject to noisy neighbor risks. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools, autoscaling policies, and tighter latency SLOs — we can commit to 95p latency targets in the contract. For your sub-200ms 95p goal with short prompts, Dedicated is a good fit; we'll want to tune batching and KV cache behavior.
[03:05] Leah: On the ops side — if we go Dedicated, what's networking look like? We need VPC peering, SSO, and KMS for encryption; some customers require no logging of prompts.
[03:16] Nina: For Dedicated we support private deployments with VPC peering or Private Link, SAML SSO, RBAC, and optional customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). Audit logs can be configured; we can also put a retention policy or opt to not store full prompt transcripts depending on contract and legal. We'll share the VPC checklist.
[03:36] Tom: Regarding cost, do you have a ballpark for reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go?
[03:41] Samir: We typically provide a few commitment tiers. Reserved capacity reduces per-token unit cost considerably, and we can model your current OpenAI spend versus a Dedicated commit. I'll put that comparison in the pricing deck.
[03:52] Marc: One technical question — we've optimized with vLLM and custom kernels for long context. How does Redwood handle long KV cache and attention optimizations?
[03:59] Jordan: Our runtime supports continuous KV caching and selects optimized kernels based on model architecture and sequence distribution. For very long contexts we use chunked attention and memory-efficient strategies — we can also recommend quantization profiles to reduce memory while preserving quality.
[04:16] Marc: Do you support 16-bit and 8-bit quantized variants out-of-box? We've seen some quality drops at 8-bit in important prompts.
[04:23] Nina: Yes, we support multiple quantization profiles. We usually recommend trying 16-bit or Q4 variants first and running evals. Our Optimize tooling suggests profiles per workload. We'll help with regression testing — if you have a set of golden prompts we can run them across quantization settings.
[04:40] Asha: On governance — SOC2, Do you have ISO? We need a SOC2 report and details on data residency for customers in EU.
[04:47] Samir: We are SOC2 Type II, and we have EU regions for data residency. For Private deployments we can offer on-prem or customer-managed cloud in their region. We'll attach SOC2 and data residency docs.
[04:58] Leah: For KMS, can we bring our key? HSM?
[05:01] Nina: Yes, customer-managed KMS is supported for Dedicated, and we integrate with major cloud KMS providers and HSM solutions for high-assurance customers.
[05:09] Marc: Any known incompatibilities migrating from OpenAI GPT-4 style prompts? Tokenization differences, role/name handling in chat messages?
[05:16] Jordan: Role/name handling is usually fine; tokenizer differences can cause subtle shifts. We map chat schema to our API and support wrappers to mimic OpenAI's responses. Also watch out for model family differences — if you're used to a particular GPT-4-like flavor, parity may require model selection or small prompt tuning.
[05:34] Tom: How fast can we run a pilot? We want to test 2-3 models and run our prompt suite.
[05:39] Samir: We can get a pilot started quickly — provision trial dedicated capacity, share the benchmark plan, and run side-by-side. Typically 1-2 weeks to provision and run the initial benchmark depending on approval. Jordan will coordinate.
[05:52] Marc: For benchmarks can you simulate our traffic shape? We have bursts that matter for tail latency.
[05:57] Jordan: Yes, we'll replay your traffic distribution and simulate bursts. We'll also instrument token-level latency.
[06:07] Asha: Any limitations on bringing proprietary models? We have some licensed weights with restrictions.
[06:12] Nina: We support private model hosting in Dedicated and for Private deployments we can ensure models never leave your network. Licensing constraints are handled on a case-by-case basis; we have an onboarding checklist for licensed weights.
[06:25] Marc: One more — function / tool calling differences. We use structured outputs a lot.
[06:31] Jordan: We support structured output and tool calling patterns; the runtime supports streaming and function-calling semantics similar to mainstream APIs. There may be small SDK differences but we provide client libraries.
[06:42] Tom: Any references or case studies of customers migrating from OpenAI?
[06:46] Samir: Yes — a couple of our enterprise customers moved to Dedicated for cost and latency reasons. I'll include a short case study in the follow-up email.
[06:55] Marc: Ok, let's talk about the evaluation metrics — beyond exact matches we care about downstream scoring.
[07:01] Jordan: We'll accept your success criteria and run both openai and redwood runs, produce diff reports, highlight drift, and recommend prompt adjustments. We can also run A/B tests behind a feature flag in your product.
[07:15] Asha: On the legal side, procurement questions — do you support SOC2 attestation, data processing addendum (DPA), and standard contract terms?
[07:23] Samir: Yes, we have standard DPAs, and our legal team supports enterprise contracts for Dedicated and Private. For very regulated customers we do custom terms.
[07:33] Leah: Network specifics — do you need outbound access to some Redwood control plane or is everything inbound?
[07:40] Nina: For Dedicated there's a lightweight control plane traffic for monitoring and billing; for Private on-prem options we can limit external connectivity and provide a local control plane option. We'll share the architecture diagram.
[07:52] Marc: Let's capture the immediate risks: eval parity, tokenization drift, and procurement lead time.
[07:58] Samir: Agreed. We'll help mitigate by running side-by-side evals and providing quick rollbacks. For procurement we'll provide a standard quote to speed approvals.
[08:08] Tom: Are there any open-source infra components we should know about (e.g., vLLM/TGI) you're relying on?
[08:13] Jordan: We integrate with those ecosystems where useful but our serving runtime is Redwood's codebase with optimized kernels. For some model types we still rely on community toolchains for conversion.
[08:25] Marc: Roughly what's the onboarding timeline to Dedicated if we decide to sign?
[08:29] Samir: Contract negotiation is variable; from signature to warm Dedicated capacity typically 2-4 weeks. Pilot can start earlier with trial capacity.
[08:38] Asha: Ok let's walk through next steps — who owns what?
[08:42] Samir: I'll follow up with pricing and the case study. Nina will share security docs, Jordan will draft the benchmark plan. Marc and Leah will provide prompts and network details.
[08:52] Marc: Sounds good.
[08:55] Tom: One last small thing — do you provide a rollback mechanism if a model causes downstream regressions in production?
[09:00] Jordan: Yes, we support canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback to a specified legacy model. You can pin a previous variant.
[09:10] Asha: Great. That's all from me.
[09:13] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and the attachments.
[09:17] [End of recording — remaining minutes used for internal Q&A]

Notes on transcript quality: rough auto-transcription; occasional proper noun mistakes (e.g., TGI spelled as 'T G I' in places), filler words present. References shared: pricing deck link (sent after), security pack (SOC2, DPA), VPC onboarding doc (https://redwood.ai/docs/dedicated-vpc), benchmark repo placeholder (to be shared).

Call recap (verbatim like at end of meeting):
Samir: Recap — Redwood to provide pricing, SOC2 + KMS docs, and a benchmark plan. Veridian to provide prompt sets and confirm network settings. We'll aim to run a side-by-side benchmark the week of 2026-03-16.

"Great, thanks everyone, talk soon."
